title: McKinnon v. Benedict
lead: A short interest-free loan secured a twenty-five-year restriction on a neighboring resort. Wisconsin’s Supreme Court refused that restriction’s equitable enforcement while preserving relief for a separate trespass.

actors.name: The Benedicts
actors.role: Buyers and operators of Bent’s Camp

actors.name: The McKinnons
actors.role: Surrounding landowners who financed part of the purchase

proceedings: County court enjoined resort changes and granted separate trespass relief.
Wisconsin Supreme Court partly reversed, partly affirmed, and remanded April 9, 1968.
limits: Specific-enforcement ruling between original parties, not a damages decision invalidating every legal contract obligation. Trespass relief survived; costs and improper-injunction damages required further proceedings.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Financing a resort purchase
paragraphs: The Benedicts wanted to buy Bent’s Camp, an approximately eighty-acre Mamie Lake resort surrounded by about 1,170 acres owned by the McKinnons. Fourteen cabins and a lodge occupied the desirable lakeside area; undeveloped land across County Trunk B was less useful. Unable to finance the $60,000 land-contract purchase fully, the buyers obtained a $5,000 loan from McKinnon.

His August 31, 1960 letter required an interest-free note secured by a first mortgage on their Michigan cottage, along with a contemplated recordable restriction on specified tree cutting and improvements closer to his property than existing buildings for twenty-five years. Land west of the road and a separate woodlot were excluded. He offered planting trees, free firewood areas, efforts to resolve Mrs. Vair’s fifty-year cabin lease at $5 annually, customers, and help organizing the business.

The Benedicts signed and repaid the advance after about seven months in spring 1961. Their seller’s land contract separately restricted use while unpaid. They spent $20,000 improving cabins between 1961 and 1964, but declining income made payments difficult. McKinnon’s lease effort failed; little business resulted, and he made no attempt to organize the operation.

sections.title: Trailer spaces prompt an injunction
sections.cue: The competing uses of the property
paragraphs: Seeking financial stability, the Benedicts developed eighteen trailer spaces in fall 1964 for about $8,000, then a tent campsite the next spring for about $1,200. When the seasonal McKinnon residents returned in June 1965, they sued under the agreement, zoning and trailer-ordinance objections, and a separate allegation of trespass on their point of land inside the surrounding resort.

After a bench trial, the county court prohibited further grading and trailer or camper rentals, restricted resort use through August 31, 1985, and purported to bind later buyers. The Benedicts appealed. Justice Heffernan’s Wisconsin Supreme Court opinion first rejected binding subsequent purchasers in what the McKinnons themselves characterized as a simple contract action between original parties. As to those parties, the issue was equitable specific enforcement; no damages action for breach had been brought.

sections.title: The burden exceeds the protected benefit
paragraphs: Inadequate damages did not automatically justify an injunction. Equity could refuse relief for grossly inadequate consideration, unfair terms, or disproportionate hardship without finding dishonesty or sharp practice. Literal enforcement would freeze the resort’s 1960 development for twenty-five years, confining even ordinary additional cottages to a narrow area. The unrestricted land across the road was least suited to expansion.

The consideration was not a $5,000 gift. Seven months’ free use of secured funds was worth about $145 at the land contract’s five-percent rate. Other promised help produced little. The buyers’ dependence on the advance demonstrated inability to bargain at arm’s length rather than curing the imbalance.

Benefits to the neighbors were small: the trailer park was invisible from their house, and summer foliage hid the tents during their main residence period. McKinnon’s $50,000 depreciation estimate was admissible but weak, especially as his expert could not quantify depreciation. Although the record showed no dishonesty or overreaching, McKinnon’s extensive legal and business experience contrasted with the retail jeweler’s position, and the buyers apparently overvalued his promises. Inadequate consideration, oppressive restrictions, limited benefit, and bargaining circumstances made equitable enforcement unfair from the outset. The court did not thereby adjudicate all possible damages obligations.

sections.title: Trespass remains a separate wrong
paragraphs: The ordinance objections supplied no independent bar to development. The ordinance and clerk’s testimony supported proper enactment; the challenged annual license had expired, mooting its location-description issue. Clerk-assisted campground language did not invalidate the application, and plans could be required at renewal.

Evidence nevertheless supported the McKinnons’ title to the lakeside point and the Benedicts’ trespass there. The court affirmed the related damages and injunction. A $750 tree-planting item restored screening previously supplied by a mound and vegetation; it did not improperly improve the owners’ position. Freedom to develop their own resort did not authorize grading someone else’s land.

The $1,355.70 counsel-fee item could not stand because it was not attributable solely to the successful trespass claim. Proper trespass-related costs and the Benedicts’ asserted damages from the improvident resort injunction remained for the trial court. The judgment was affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded: contractual equitable restraint failed, trespass relief survived.
